entries.content:
Florian Haubner

Industry Architect Lead Automotive

Per Sigurdson

CEO & co-founder, RemotiveLabs

Imagining traditional gearheads getting their hands on software-defined vehicles is an amusing thought experiment. With their socket wrenches and air compressors at the ready, they might be confused to encounter core functions more likely to run on 1s and 0s than oil and belts. But across the auto industry these days, more and more vehicles feature prominent systems built using cloud-native development, continuous integration/continuous delivery, fast digital iteration, and plenty of AI.

But there’s still a big gap to be found in many automakers’ and Tier 1 suppliers’ cloud-based development processes. On the one hand, these companies are commonly using software to develop vehicles’ digital entertainment and information screens, or other onboard high-performance computers.

On the other, the dozens of microchips and control modules that make a car a car these days — such as gateways, body controllers, zone control units, sensor and actuator nodes — are still frequently hardwired to physical chips when they’re constructed, making them very difficult to update, reprogram, or expand after the vehicle drives off the factory floor. Teams have to wait for benches, samples, and rigs, and integration can easily slip to the end of the development process, where defects are most expensive to fix.

This inherent inefficiency has become a leading bottleneck. After all, manufacturers can’t really claim vehicles are software-defined if most of their electronics only function when connected to physical hardware and if developers are leaning heavily on actual hardware.

With Horizon, our agentic innovation platform for developing software-defined vehicles, our vision is to help manufacturers avoid these inefficiencies by working with partners like RemotiveLabs.

The cockpit already runs in the cloud

The Android team has invested a significant amount of time and effort over the last few years on enabling seamless development of the many digital systems in vehicles’ cockpits. Android Automotive OS (AAOS) runs inside Google’s official virtual testing environment for Android, Cuttlefish, which itself runs comfortably on Arm-based Google Cloud instances. With this approach, developers can build, boot, and test virtual versions of their infotainment stacks on the same Arm architecture that ships in vehicles.

And with the recent launch of Android 17 and AAOS SDV, this capability is also extended to further domains, whenever AAOS SDV is used. Deploying it with Cuttlefish, for example, proves the model: representative software, on representative architecture, in the cloud, on demand. The question that still needs to be answered is how to extend that model to the rest of the vehicle, especially when other operating systems are involved.

The harness around the virtual vehicle

That’s where RemotiveTopology comes into play. As the harness around the virtual vehicle, it’s the layer that connects AAOS in Cuttlefish to a full, simulated electrical and electronic (E/E) architecture: the rest of the vehicle’s onboard computers, its data networks, and the live signals that make the system function like a real vehicle rather than a collection of standalone apps.

RemotiveTopology automatically utilizes manufacturers’ existing network design files to build a working, virtual version of their cars’ networks. This is vehicle-as-code: the E/E architecture expressed as an executable specification, versioned and provisioned like infrastructure-as-code. In this way, an entire vehicle can be spun up on demand. Cockpit software talks to the rest of the vehicle exactly as it would in a real vehicle. As a result, developers get full and continuous signal and cross-domain visibility, so they can see real-time system status. And because it is built on standard Linux tooling, the same topology runs on a laptop and in a contiguous integration pipeline on Google Cloud.

Integrate across domains early, not late

The payoff for using this approach is that all onboard systems can be developed and integrated with software before any of them are connected to a vehicle’s hardware. That’s beneficial because the most difficult (and latest) integration in a vehicle’s development is bringing all its systems together. For example, advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) produce object lists, trajectories, and mode requests that the cockpit has to render and react to, while the infotainment system and information cluster have to reflect driving state while body and chassis nodes sit in the loop.

With the full topology live on Google Cloud, the infotainment system and ADAS can operate simultaneously within a virtual vehicle, exchanging real signals over the simulated network. This means it’s possible to exercise handoffs like an ADAS event surfacing in the cluster or a driver-mode change rippling across domains from day one in continuous integration long before the benches and samples line up. In this way, developers can be confident they’ll discover multi-domain integration long before the end of the process so that they can test continuously from the start.

The full vehicle frontier

At the heart of this work is a shared desire to bring scalable software development to even the smallest and most common nodes in a vehicle, its microchips and control modules. That’s because these are the parts that have traditionally been wired to hardware, and as a result are the biggest blocker to fully software-defined vehicles.

The ultimate goal is that the same software that runs in the cloud can run on vehicles’ actual control modules with no re-tooling or re-validation needed to move between them. That parity is natural with Arm-based Google Cloud infrastructure because the cloud and the car share an instruction set. Google's Axion makes it straightforward: C4A metal, a bare-metal Arm instance, is provided explicitly for automotive systems development and Android software development, giving direct hardware access without unnecessary software layers and delivering the consistent performance that vehicle systems require.

Taken together, this holistic system allows teams, for the first time, to develop and integration-test an entire vehicle’s systems in the cloud and then apply it to the actual vehicle without having to rewrite it.

Why now, and where to start

The payoff is not abstract. Treating the vehicle as code and moving integration into the cloud compresses the slowest, most expensive phase of a program. Early customer engagements with RemotiveLabs have measured more than 10x faster integration cycles. And the development loop is now changing faster than the hardware loop: AI-assisted and agentic workflows can rapidly generate, test, and refine vehicle software, but only virtual systems provide the required scale. Every element that can’t be virtualized can slow the entire development process down.

RemotiveTopology provides this architecture as vehicle-as-code and makes it accessible for developers, testers, and autonomous AI agents alike. Best of all, there is no new third-party tooling to adopt just to get started. Instead, RemotiveLabs publishes an open-source simplified vehicle on GitHub that anyone can run in minutes on standard Linux tooling and platform definitions already in place. Full existing toolchains plug in as a manufacturer or Tier1 supplier scales, and RemotiveTopology can be easily dropped into an Arm-based Google Cloud environment.

For those building software-defined vehicles whose virtual development stops at the cockpit, it’s time to start with an open-source example, bring unique platform definitions, and run an entire vehicle in the cloud. RemotiveTopology is available in Horizon for easy usage in combination with other Horizon modules.

We are announcing  a new logging feature that  is now available in Python User-Defined Function (UDF) in BigQuery. Developers can now use Python’s standard logging library directly inside BigQuery UDFs to emit structured logs seamlessly into Cloud Logging—with zero external plugins or custom connectors required.

While UDF logging enables a wide range of operational monitoring and debugging workflows, to demonstrate this feature we are showcasing an example for building fault-tolerant, resilient data pipelines. In the example below, we are capturing row-level diagnostic telemetry during query execution, so that teams can easily isolate problematic records, trigger real-time alerts, and triage issues via SQL without halting entire workloads.

In this post, we’ll show you how to get started with Python UDF logging and walk through an e-commerce event ingestion pipeline as a practical, end-to-end example.

    _AllLogs
    view, diagnose the root cause, and re-ingest recovered data.

Other use cases

  • Shadow execution & safe migrations: Run legacy and new business logic side-by-side in a UDF. Return the legacy result to production while logging calculation differences to Cloud Logging.

  • Cost management: On high-throughput pipelines, log selectively (e.g., only on errors or via sampling) to manage logging ingestion volume.

entries.content:
Héctor González Álvarez

Senior Technical Solutions Consultant, Google Cloud

Is your LLM-as-a-judge truly objective?

There’s a common misconception in tech that humans are subjective, so we should rely on AI for objective evaluation. But the reality is that LLMs are also subjective. Just like human reviewers, they can carry biases:

  • Verbosity bias: LLM judges usually favor longer, confident-sounding answers, even when the underlying facts are wrong.
  • Position bias: Swapping the order of two options can cause an LLM judge to flip its verdict over 75% of the time.
  • The halo effect: Because LLMs generate text piece by piece, clean grammar and formatting can trick an AI judge into giving top marks for accuracy while missing errors.
  • Agreeableness bias: LLM judges are great at recognizing valid work. But with detecting errors, they may fail to catch incorrect, buggy, or unsafe outputs up to 75% of the time.
  • Self-enhancement bias: Also known as egocentric bias, AI evaluators systematically overrate outputs that were generated by themselves or from their own family.

Ultimately, LLM judges are not objective arbiters of truth. They are subjective models with their own distinct biases. Treating them as infallible tools that don't need their quality measured might leave your work compromised.

In this post, we’ll explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality.

Three helpful ways to audit your LLM judges

Pillar 1: Measure internal stability

Before you can trust an AI judge’s score, you need to know that it isn't just guessing. Because LLMs are probabilistic, they can be inconsistent, giving different scores to the exact same text.

You can test this internal stability by running multi-pass consistency checks on a single output and calculating the variance. If a judge's scores fluctuate wildly on identical inputs, its rubric is too ambiguous.

Pillar 2: Validate human alignment

When your evaluation datasets are mostly valid responses, a lenient AI judge can look great on paper. It might align closely with human reviewers overall, but miss a majority of invalid or even unsafe outputs.

To prove your LLM judge is catching real errors, you need chance-corrected metrics. These mathematical models filter out agreements driven purely by leniency or random chance, showing how closely your evaluator actually aligns with the informed decisions of human experts.

Pillar 3: Use multi-judge ensembles

To avoid the halo effect mentioned earlier, teams should use decomposed prompting. Instead of asking one LLM judge to score an entire response, assign a specialized judge to evaluate a single criteria, like factual accuracy or tone. This isolates traits and forces independent scoring.

Second, to track performance in real time without human intervention, the established best practice is ensembling. This means running at least two different models under the hood to evaluate the exact same output simultaneously.

By finding the statistical consensus between these models, you can flag if their evaluations begin to diverge and avoid any scoring quality degradation.

entries.content:
Dave Wang

Forward Deployed Engineer, Google Cloud

Enterprise assistants still respond mostly in text. However, that can break down for visual, multi-step work, where every adjustment costs another slow chat turn.

MCP Apps (SEP-1865) solves this. This open Model Context Protocol (MCP) extension pairs a tool with a live UI. In Gemini Enterprise, that UI renders directly in the chat flow inside a sandboxed iframe, and can expand to fullscreen or a side panel. Edits run locally while the workspace and assistant stay synchronized.

You also avoid rebuilding core foundations: Gemini provides workforce sign-in, governed data access, and the Default Assistant, while you host your MCP server on a private Cloud Run service.

Why we need MCP Apps

Enterprise assistants have evolved through three generations:

  • Generation 1 (Text chatbots): Returns static markdown with no interactive controls.

  • Generation 2 (Standard MCP tools): Invokes live APIs, but outputs static text. Every change requires another model turn.

  • Generation 3 (Interactive MCP Apps): Pairs each tool with a live workspace. Adjustments happen in the widget without a model turn, while the assistant stays in sync.

Building MCP Apps in Gemini delivers six benefits:

  • Responsive user experience: Single-click actions execute directly in the panel without round-tripping through the chat.

  • Purpose-built workflows: Deliver visual redaction views for legal review, 3D viewers for CAD, or sensitivity models for finance.

  • Enterprise security: Workforce OAuth sign-in, private Cloud Run ingress, and a sandboxed iframe protect every layer.

  • Human-in-the-loop governance: Experts inspect and approve high-stakes actions before execution.

  • Open standard: Portable across compatible hosts, with automatic text fallback.

  • Broad connectivity: Connect to BigQuery, Agent Platform, Cloud Storage, or internal ERP and CRM systems.

High-level architecture

Three decoupled tiers work together:

  • Client browser: Shows the chat alongside the MCP App widget in the side panel.

  • Gemini Enterprise: The default assistant calls tools, the AppBridge proxy relays widget messages, and the connector manages OAuth.

  • Google Cloud (your project): You deploy and host the MCP server on Cloud Run, which exposes one JSON-RPC endpoint (/mcp), runs background jobs, and serves the single-file HTML widget.

Each tier talks only to its neighbor, letting Gemini Enterprise enforce security and routing.

Authentication with two independent layers

Each user signs in through OAuth 2.0. On every call, Gemini Enterprise sends its service agent token alongside the user's OAuth token:

  • Layer 1 (Cloud Run IAM): Enforced at Google's edge, this answers "which service may call?" Public access is disabled; unauthorized callers receive HTTP 403.

  • Layer 2 (In-App OAuth): Enforced inside the application, this answers "which user is calling?" Failed verification returns HTTP 401, prompting the user to sign in again.

Cloud Run IAM cannot distinguish end users, so both layers are required. Outbound calls use a least-privilege service account.

Build, deploy on Google Cloud, and register in Gemini Enterprise

First, build your custom MCP server (exposing POST /mcp and a bundled ui:// HTML widget) using the MCP Apps SDK, or use Google Antigravity  to scaffold and deploy your MCP App with this starter prompt:

  • Build an MCP App for Gemini Enterprise using the create-mcp-app skill (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/tree/main/plugins/mcp-apps/skills/create-mcp-app).

  • Workflow: [describe your input data, side-panel UI controls, and approval or export actions].

  • Generate a single-file HTML widget, a Streamable HTTP backend (POST /mcp) with <2s async tool responses and get_app_state polling, and Cloud Run deployment commands (--no-allow-unauthenticated, --no-cpu-throttling, --min-instances=1).

Once your MCP server code is ready, deploy it to Cloud Run and connect it to Gemini Enterprise:

  • Step 1: Enable APIs for Cloud Run, Discovery Engine, Agent Platform, and Organization Policy.

  • Step 2: Deploy your MCP server container to Cloud Run from source 

    (gcloud run deploy  --source .
    ) with 
    --no-allow-unauthenticated, --no-cpu-throttling
    so background work does not freeze between polls, and --min-instances=1.

  • Step 3: Grant the invoker role (

    roles/run.invoker
    ) to your Discovery Engine service agent (Layer 1).
  • Step 4: Create an OAuth 2.0 Web Client with redirect URI 
    https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/oauth-redirect
    (Layer 2).

  • Step 5: Override the 

    discoveryengine.managed.disableCustomMcpServerConnector
    constraint and complete the Before you begin prerequisites 
    (roles/discoveryengine.editor
    for the admin, allowedEgressFqdns for your server and OAuth hosts, and 
    custom_mcp
    in 
    allowedDataSources
    if enforced). Then, in the Google Cloud Console under Gemini Enterprise > Data stores > Create data store, select Custom MCP Server and register the connector:

  • Step 6: Enable actions on your data store. Gemini Enterprise imports your MCP server's tools as actions and disables them by default. In the Cloud Console, open Gemini Enterprise > Data stores > [Your MCP Data Store] > Actions, click Reload custom actions (which calls 

    tools/list
    on your server), select your model-visible tools, and click Enable actions.
  • Step 7: Connect the data store to your app. Open Gemini Enterprise > Apps > [Your App] > Connected data stores > Add existing data stores, and select your MCP data store. Connecting it as a data store gives the built-in Default Assistant access to your MCP tools and UI widget directly in main chat ( do not use "Add Agent,"  which is for external sub-agents rather than MCP data stores).

Build your own

An MCP App pairs backend tools with a live workspace in Gemini Enterprise. You do not build a chat frontend or identity pipeline; you deploy one Cloud Run container and attach it as a Data Store, making Gemini Enterprise where enterprise work gets done.

  • Co-build with Google Antigravity here

  • Build on Google Cloud: MCP Apps Specification (SEP-1865), Cloud Run, and Google Cloud AI.

entries.content:
Jamie de Guerre

Senior Director, Outbound Product Management

As organizations work to leverage AI to transform their businesses, it is clear that the raw model intelligence is not the key challenge.

Consistently, we hear that the challenges lie in how the agents can be deployed across the company while meeting key requirements for quality, integration, security, and governance.

Gemini provides that connected foundation across the enterprise, and it’s why we believe Google was named a Leader in the inaugural IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment1.

IDC MarketScape vendor analysis model is designed to provide an overview of the competitive fitness of technology and suppliers in a given market. The research methodology utilizes a rigorous scoring methodology based on both qualitative and quantitative criteria that results in a single graphical illustration of each supplier’s position within a given market. The Capabilities score measures supplier product, go-to-market and business execution in the short-term. The Strategy score measures alignment of supplier strategies with customer requirements in a 3-5 year timeframe. Supplier market share is represented by the size of the icons.

Gemini meets work where it already happens

A viable agentic platform has to meet work where it already happens – and run under production-grade controls. Gemini is engineered to deliver developer velocity without compromising governance, built around four core differentiators:

1. Surfaces that connect builders and business teams

Gemini makes it so that every surface connects back to one universal foundation.

  • Where teams already work: Employees collaborate with Gemini directly inside Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or team chats – the agent carries the same persistent memory, skills, and enterprise permissions across desktop and mobile without needing to switch tools.
  • Builder tools centered on choice: Gemini platform supports how developers want to work, spanning no-code and low-code builders in the studio to code-first workflows with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) and Antigravity.
  • Workflows that compound across the organization: When a team solves a complex workflow, they can package it into a shared skill published to a central Agent Registry. Gemini calls on these skills directly to execute tasks, turning proven procedures into reusable assets across the entire company.

2. Radical openness across models, enterprise data, and tools

Gemini adapts to the software you already run, not the other way around.

  • Model choice: Through Model Garden in Gemini platform, teams have direct access to over 200 models – including all of the breakthroughs from Google DeepMind like Gemini 4 Argon, day one access to the latest Anthropic models, and third-party and open models.
  • Grounding on your enterprise data: Gemini connects directly to live enterprise data across Google Cloud in BigQuery and Cloud Storage, as well as Salesforce, SAP, and others. Because Gemini inherits each employee's existing credentials, sensitive information stays governed at the source.
  • Open standards: Built on open protocols like MCP and A2A, Gemini can easily plug into your existing toolchains and communicate across multi-vendor environments.

3. Smarter token economics

Gemini optimizes cost, latency, and performance directly at the execution layer.

  • Matching tasks to the right model: By default, Gemini uses Auto mode for users, letting the platform match each step of a task to the right model dynamically. It defaults to a fast workhorse model like Gemini Flash, and escalates to a high-capacity frontier reasoning model only when task complexity requires it.
  • Reusable skills: Teams can package proven processes into shared skills. Your agents can execute against these established procedures, improving consistency and reducing repetitive token consumption across the company.
  • Budget guardrails: Administrators can set spending limits by project, department, or individual agent in the billing console. When a budget threshold is reached, new requests pause while active tasks are allowed to complete, giving finance and engineering predictable cost controls without abruptly interrupting in-progress work.

4. Built-in governance and security

Gemini incorporates enterprise governance natively, and at no additional cost.

  • Dedicated agent identity: Every agent receives its own distinct, authenticated identity governed by least-privilege permissions. When an agent takes action, every event is recorded in an audit trail tied directly to that identity and the identity of which user was using the agent for the task.
  • Isolated sandboxes: A sandboxed boundary keeps dynamic tasks strictly contained, protecting your underlying infrastructure, core network, and sensitive corporate data from being exposed or compromised.
  • Policy enforcement: Rather than relying on a model to self-police, Agent Gateway automatically applies corporate security policies, blocks data leakage, and ensures agents only access what they are explicitly authorized to touch.

Looking forward

At its core, Gemini is all about giving your organization an open, reliable platform where builders have choice and teams work with complete confidence.

We are honored by IDC MarketScape’s recognition of Google as a Leader, and we look forward to continuing this work alongside our customers.

Download the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment excerpt to learn why Google is named a Leader.

1. SOURCE: “Worldwide Agentic AI Platforms 2026 Vendor Assessment”, October 2026, IDC # US54140926.

entries.content:
Injae Kwak

AI Infrastructure Product Manager

Shivaji Dutta

AI Infra Solutions Architect

Today, Reflection released Beam, its first open-weight model built to give developers, researchers, and enterprises open control and customization for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by solving complex reasoning and coding problems with 3x to 4x higher reasoning compute efficiency than comparable open models.

Alongside today’s release, Google Cloud is announcing day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for serving Beam on Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure.

To help developers get the full benefit of Beam’s token efficiency in production, we worked with Reflection to optimize performance of the underlying serving stack using llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang) on Google Cloud:

"By deploying our Beam model on Google Cloud, we achieved up to 5x higher performance and 8x lower latency to optimize serving of agentic workloads." - Joe Spisak, VP of Product & Head of Open Source, Reflection

With today’s day 0 release on Google Cloud, developers get:

  • Compounding model and system efficiency: Combining Beam’s 3x to 4x reasoning compute efficiency with system-level optimizations on A4X Max instances (NVIDIA GB300 NVL72) for up to 5x higher throughput and 8x lower latency,* and G4 VMs (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) for up to 2x higher throughput and 8x lower latency.*

  • High-efficiency multi-turn serving: KV-cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, speculative decoding and hierarchical KV cache offloading to Host DRAM and Local SSD reduce redundant prompt recomputation across long coding sessions.

  • Turnkey optimized deployment: Our recommended performance optimized recipes for agentic workloads with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo are available in AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes, llm-d repo and Model Garden in Gemini platformwith a few clicks. 

*Based on customer benchmarking

Scaling inference requires system-level optimization

When evaluating models for agentic coding and tool use, inference efficiency happens at two distinct layers: how efficiently the model reasons and how efficiently the serving system executes multi-turn loops.

Model-level efficiency: Reflection’s Beam

Reflection designed Beam (~501B total parameters with ~23B active parameters per token, and an approximately 1M-token context window) specifically for text-native software engineering and multi-step tool use. It plugs directly into the coding harnesses developers already use, including Reflection’s Mirror CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, and , to resolve GitHub issues, run CLI and DevOps workflows, and complete long-horizon tasks.

Because Beam activates only 23B parameters per token and reaches solutions using 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens than other comparable open weight models, it dramatically reduces the inference-time compute required for each reasoning step.

System-level efficiency: AI Hypercomputer optimized serving

Once developers deploy an agent into production, a second set of bottlenecks could appear at the serving layer. In an agentic coding loop, the model is called dozens of times in a single session. With every turn, the coding harness appends new file reads, code diffs, compiler logs, and tool outputs to a shared conversation history that quickly grows to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens.

Even when the model itself generates 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens on each turn, the accumulated context window across turns creates two major infrastructure challenges:

First, prefill compute becomes a bottleneck. Standard Kubernetes load balancers distribute requests using stateless round-robin routing. When a coding harness sends Turn 15 of a session, it often lands on a different replica than Turn 14. That replica is forced to recompute the entire historical prompt from scratch, wasting GPU compute and creating long prefill queues that delay other users.

Second, decode becomes bottlenecked by KV cache capacity. Holding long-context KV caches for dozens of concurrent agent sessions quickly fills up GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, the serving engine has to evict older KV blocks. As soon as those blocks are evicted, cache hit rates drop and GPU throughput stalls.

To preserve Beam’s model-level efficiency at cluster scale, the serving stack has to be optimized as a distributed system. That is why our recipes pair Beam with llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang).

Inside the AI Hypercomputer inference architecture

To run Beam’s BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints at peak efficiency on Day 0, we designed a vertically integrated architecture on AI Hypercomputer where each layer handles a specific part of the agentic serving lifecycle.

System optimized architecture for serving agentic traffic

Rather than treating inference pods as stateless endpoints, each layer of the stack is co-designed around the multi-turn agent lifecycle:

  • Prefix- and load-aware routing (GKE + llm-d EPP / Dynamo router): Tracks cached prefixes and queue depth across worker pods, steering each follow-up turn from a coding harness to the replica holding its warm KV prefix while preventing queue saturation via turn-priority flow control.

  • Disaggregated compute and speculative decoding (A4X Max & G4 instance): Runs vLLM and SGLang with native Blackwell NVFP4, Expert Parallelism (EP) for Beam’s 23B active experts, Data-Parallel Attention, and DFlash2 speculative decoding. Separating Prefill and Decode (P/D) pools ensures heavy prompt bursts never stall active token generation.

  • Tiered KV cache (GPU Memory -> DRAM & Local SSD) Active KV blocks stay in high-bandwidth GPU memory (Tier 1), while warm KV blocks evicted during long-horizon sessions overflow into host CPU DRAM and local NVMe SSDs (Tier 2) via vLLM’s OffloadingConnector or SGLang's HiCache, allowing historical context to be fetched in milliseconds instead of recomputed from scratch.

System optimizations for multi-turn agentic workloads

When serving multi-turn coding and tool-use workloads like the AgentX trajectory dataset across rising concurrency levels, each layer in the serving stack contributes to the performance and latency improvements for multi-turn, long context traffic patterns of agentic workloads:

A note on reading these charts. The two configurations are not comparable to each other. NVIDIA Dynamo ran on A4X Max instances with 32 x NVIDIA GB300 NVL72GPUs; llm-d ran on G4 VMs with 8 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Each chart shows the gain over a baseline on the same hardware. More replicas give the router more warm KV caches to hit and more room to split prefill from decode, so the uplift grows with the deployment. Both llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo scale up and down to match the underlying infrastructure.

NVIDIA Dynamo optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam

llm-d optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam

Across both platforms, layering these optimizations shifts the Pareto frontier to deliver higher output throughput and faster per-user interactivity simultaneously:

  • Baseline deployment (Stateless round-robin routing). In a standard Kubernetes deployment without prefix awareness, consecutive turns from the same coding session land on different replicas, forcing constant prefill recomputation on historical context and causing throughput to plateau as concurrency scales.

  • KV-cache-aware & flow control routing. Enabling prefix-aware routing in NVIDIA Dynamo or llm-d’s Sticky EPP with turn-priority flow control keeps multi-turn agent trajectories pinned to the replica holding their warm KV cache, immediately cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency and freeing up GPU compute, resulting in a significant increase in token throughput.

  • Host DRAM and Local SSD (LSSD) KV offloading. Offloading evicted KV blocks from GPU memory into host DRAM and local NVMe SSDs prevents cache thrashing when dozens of long-context coding sessions exceed on-device GPU memory capacity.

  • Disaggregated serving, speculative decoding, and KV pool tuning. Tuning hybrid KV cache memory allocation, enabling speculative decoding, and disaggregating prefill and decode workers isolates token generation from heavy prompt bursts while the draft model multiplies output throughput to keep per-agent token interactivity fast.

Get started and meet us at PyTorchCon and GTC Berlin

This blog explored how you can leverage system level optimizations to scale performance to serve Reflection's Beam family of models for agentic workloads. All of the Kubernetes manifests, router configurations, and benchmarking scripts from this post are open-source and ready to run on your own GKE cluster.

  • Deploy the optimized stack: Explore the day 0 guides for running Reflection’s Beam with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo in the AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes repository on A4X Max and G4, and Model Garden in Gemini platform.
  • Download the weights: Grab the Apache 2.0 BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints on Reflection’s Hugging Face page.
  • Visit us at the llm-d and PyTorch Conference in San Jose: If you are attending PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose this October, stop by the llm-d community sessions and the Google Cloud booth #. We will be walking through live demos of KV-cache-aware routing, P/D disaggregation, and KV cache tiering for agentic workloads.
  • Come see us at NVIDIA GTC Berlin: If you are attending NVIDIA GTC Berlin, come connect with us at our booth #3026, or our Google Cloud Hub at w3.hub: just a short 5 minute walk from the venue. Learn more about our sessions.

Oct 12 - Oct 16

  • AI tokenomics in action: Enforcing tiered token budgets with Apigee

    Scaling artificial intelligence across an enterprise requires clear token governance to keep LLM spend predictable across departments. Join Tarun Abraham on Thursday, November 5, 2026 for a Community TechTalk on AI tokenomics. Discover how to use Apigee to enforce isolated, tiered token budgets and model access for each team—such as assigning Engineering a dedicated budget for Gemini Pro while covering mixed usage for Marketing—without changing application code. Attendees will also gain access to a sample codebase featuring a reusable Shared Flow.

    Register for the November 5 Community TechTalk

Sept 28 - Oct 2

  • Claude Sonnet 5.5 is now available on Google Cloud. Built for focused coding and knowledge work, it delivers stronger performance for feature development, and creating presentation-ready documents, while offering more intelligence with a lower cost per task for most work at faster speed.

    Deploy Sonnet 5.5 directly from Model Garden with Google Cloud’s enterprise security, scale, and governance built in. Try it now.

    In our new blog, explore practical strategies to modernize storage operations using Storage Intelligence Advisor and enhanced Batch Operations. See how customers like Shipt and Palo Alto Networks are using these features to manage their estates at scale. Today, Storage Intelligence is used by 25 of the top 50 GCS customers. 2 in 3 customers have Storage Intelligence enabled for over 90% of their storage footprint.

    Explore best practices on our blog

    Generative AI deployments face a harsh cost-performance trade-off: static model selection either wastes budget or compromises quality. Discover how to build an Intelligent AI Gateway using Apigee X to dynamically evaluate prompt complexity in real-time. This new blueprint automatically routes simple queries to lightweight models (like Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite) and complex reasoning tasks to advanced models (like Gemini 3.7 Flash), achieving over 70% cost savings without sacrificing output quality.

    Read the guide to optimize your Gen AI architecture

    A new episode of the AI Agent Clinic is now available showing organizations how to move past manual "vibe checks" to build robust, production-grade agent evaluations. In this hands-on session, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) take DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent, and build an end-to-end eval pipeline in under an hour. Learn how to standardize multi-turn traces across any framework using OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, pair LLM judges with deterministic checkers, and catch silent quality regressions before shipping.

    Watch here

    Every enterprise plans to adopt agentic AI within two years, but data bottlenecks hold them back—AI accesses just 45% of enterprise data today (MIT, 2026). Google's Agentic Data Cloud provides the trustworthy foundation and real-time context AI needs.Join our product leaders November 4th to explore the latest innovations across databases, analytics, business intelligence, and storage, and get direct answers in our executive Q&A with Google Data Cloud VP & GM Andi Gutmans.

    Register today!

    While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solves interoperability for autonomous AI agents, chained actions like CRM edits or database queries quickly expose systems to unauthorized execution. Join our technical deep dive on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 5:00 PM CEST featuring Christophe from Google Cloud. Learn how positioning Apigee between MCP clients and enterprise backends enables fine-grained authorization (FGA), complete audit trails, and policy evaluation via emerging standards like OpenID AuthZEN.

    Language and accessibility note: This session will be hosted in French, but non-French speakers can follow along seamlessly by turning on Google Meet live translated captions to read in English, Spanish, German, Portuguese, or Italian.

    Register for the October 1 Community TechTalk

The guide covers end-to-end instructions for capturing debug traces in both Google Cloud Apigee X (or Hybrid) and the local Apigee Emulator, extracting trace JSON data via the web UI or automated REST APIs, and analyzing execution flows, variable mutations, and latency bottlenecks using the open source Apigee Trace Viewer.

    Read the Apigee Trace Viewer guide today.

Learn to run tests locally, integrate them into CI/CD pipelines, and deploy on Google Cloud Run for shared sandboxes. This approach provides instant feedback and zero cloud costs, helping teams speed up deployment cycles.

Discover how Apigee API Hub provides a central discovery surface to eliminate agent sprawl across tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and enterprise APIs. Learn how to turn existing backend services into secure MCP tools using Agent Gateway guardrails, while applying semantic caching and intelligent model routing to keep compounding token costs predictable.

    Join Google Cloud in Chicago in Oct.15 for The AI Evolution.Reserve your seat for Chicago

Join Nigel Walters on Thursday, October 8, 2026, at 5:00 PM CEST for a Community TechTalk on shift-left testing for Apigee. Discover how to use the Apigee Local Emulator and apigee-emulator-service to run sub-second assertion suites on local machines, automate CI/CD checks in GitHub Actions, and deploy ephemeral preview sandboxes on Google Cloud Run.

Built for everyday complex tasks, it delivers stronger agentic coding, research, and analysis while handling long-running work at a lower cost per token. Google Cloud continues to provide enterprise customers with broad model choice to build, deploy, and scale their AI agents securely.

Join our session on Thursday, September 24, featuring Apigee Product Manager Geir Sjurseth. Public clusters unlock use cases like IoT devices, retail storefronts, and telco network towers. Enable public access on new or existing clusters via the Google Cloud console, gcloud CLI, or REST API. Spin up your first public cluster, or reach out to kafka-hotline@google.com with questions.

Power your AI workloads, from model telemetry to real-time context engineering, without the overhead of managing complicated ETL pipelines. Built to be dependable, with native support for dead-letter topics. Try the feature today!

Sept 7 - Sept 10

    Moving voice agents to production demands robust quality monitoring. This guide dives deep into the inner workings of the Agent Development Kit (ADK) responsible for audio session auditing. Learn how the ADK's
    save_live_blob
    feature intercepts, buffers, and stores raw audio chunks during active Gemini Live sessions. We explore building an automated post-processing pipeline to seamlessly stitch these fragments into cohesive, playable audio files. Discover how to leverage these vital audio audit trails to monitor real-world interactions, diagnose failures, and ensure enterprise-grade reliability. Read the full guide here.

The AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM orchestrator offers a new way to manage PostgreSQL-compatible workloads on bare metal or VM platforms, combining the high performance of AlloyDB, access to generative AI features and Gemini models to build AI agents and applications, and full automation. The orchestrator simplifies cluster provisioning and lifecycle management by allowing you to define reference architecture specifications, customizable by adjusting instance parameters, node configurations, and networking options — discover all details in full blog post.

    Google Cloud VM Extension Manager is now generally available, eliminating the need for custom startup scripts to manage guest OS extensions across Compute Engine fleets. Define declarative, project-wide policies that enforce desired software states across all regions and zones. Benefit from continuous drift detection with automatic self-healing, multi-zone phased rollouts with automated rollbacks on failure, and centralized fleet health visibility integrated with Cloud Monitoring.

    ExploreVM Extension Manager documentation

    Planning a migration to Apigee X or Hybrid? You can now assess your legacy Apigee Edge SaaS or OPDK environment earlier in your planning cycle. Using the updated --skip-target-validation flag in the Apigee Migration Assessment Tool, teams can generate a full inventory and establish scope baselines before target infrastructure or IAM credentials are provisioned.

    Read the guide to learn more.

    Anthropic also announced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a solution that gives customers the option to safely deploy Anthropic’s most capable models while storing their data in cloud infrastructure they control.

It supports reasoning, function calling, and structured output for multi-step agentic workflows, and accepts text and image input.

    Get started today

    AI agents offer incredible productivity gains, but granting them access to read emails, query databases, and trigger APIs introduces critical new security risks. Traditional tools are no longer enough to handle automated threats like prompt injection and dynamic permissions. Discover how forward-thinking enterprises are using secure-by-default design, agent identity governance, and human-in-the-loop controls to deploy agents with confidence.

This feature allows users to leverage functions like JOINs, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals.
  • Try out our feature here and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com!

The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Tryour quickstart today!

Compete for your share of $190,000 in prizes, cash, and Google Cloud credits! Submissions are open from August 3, 2026, to August 31, 2026.

entries.content:
Schneider Larbi

Sr. Manager, Global Partner Technical Architecture

Chelsie Czop

Sr. Product Manager, AI Infrastructure

In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way.

Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks.

Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech.

A three-layer pattern

The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery.

Figure 1 — The three-layer pattern: a cognitive orchestrator (brain), a scalable GPU execution layer (muscle), and an enterprise governance plane.

The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution

The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run:

  • Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter

  • Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints

In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol. Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM).

To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture:

  • Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node.

  • Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference.

  • Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure.

This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput.

In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody.

Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC. The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter.

The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning

With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime, within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. 

Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report”, the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below;

  • In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent.
  • Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage. Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down.
  • Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. 
  • Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated.

By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads.

Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines

Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts:

The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy

Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: 

  • Agent Identity: Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. 

  • Agent Gateway: This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. 

  • Agent Registry: This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. 

  • Model Armor: This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. 

The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project.

In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways;

Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher.

Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off.

The pattern, and the path forward

High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways:

  • Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models.

  • Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage.

  • Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight.

As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable.

Reach out to your Google sales representative if you have any requirements to build a use case like this and we will be happy to talk and support you in your agent development journey on Google Cloud.

Shahar Yakov

Product Team Lead, Wiz

Everything is moving faster in the age of AI, and that includes security threats. What used to take attackers weeks to exploit can now happen in just a few minutes.

Standard vulnerability scans that run on artifacts at rest can catch basic setup issues, but to detect an attack that's actively happening you need real-time runtime protection.

Today, we’re introducing the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), in preview. This built-in integration brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's industry-leading eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters.

The operational friction of runtime security

Security and platform engineering teams share common dilemmas when deploying in-cluster runtime defenses:

  • Deployment and lifecycle friction: Deploying runtime agents often requires managing installations from third-party sources across dozens or hundreds of clusters.

  • Credential sprawl and security risks: Passing and rotating API keys as Kubernetes Secrets introduces administrative overhead and security risk.

  • Fleet-wide enforcement gaps: Platform teams lack built-in policy controls to enforce that every new cluster has runtime sensors enabled before workloads are deployed and start receiving traffic.

  • Performance and operational overhead: Without explicit and strategic resource limits, runtime agents can impact how much CPU and memory is available for your workloads and system functionality.

With the Wiz Runtime Sensor for GKE, Google Cloud and Wiz have minimized these operational barriers. The Runtime Sensor is now available in GKE as a first-party, managed platform add-on.

Bridging the gap with Wiz Runtime Sensor for GKE

The Wiz Runtime Sensor for GKE connects central security and platform engineering workflows by simplifying and automating the sensor lifecycle.

Figure 1: High-level architecture showing credential sync, sensor deployment, and threat telemetry.

With the add-on, GKE manages the sensor deployment, credential injection, and lifecycle updates. Building runtime protection directly into the platform reduces administrative overhead and provides the following benefits for your Kubernetes fleet:

Native Secret Manager integration: Security teams no longer need to distribute Wiz API keys across cluster namespaces. The add-on uses GKE's Secret Manager secret sync integration to store your Wiz credentials in an off-cluster, centralized credential vault that only a dedicated service account can access. 

GKE automatically retrieves the credentials and injects them directly into the Runtime Sensor pods. Updating a key in Secret Manager automatically syncs to the sensor without requiring cluster restarts or manual intervention.

  • Simplified enablement: After you add your Wiz credentials to Secret Manager, platform operators can enable the Runtime Sensor add-on by using the gcloud CLI or the GKE API. The GKE control plane handles deploying the sensor components, managing the lifecycle of pods, and configuring the nodes.
  • Secure egress and proxy support: For environments that restrict public internet access, the managed sensor supports standard HTTP and mTLS proxy configurations. Telemetry is routed back to Wiz without violating your egress firewall policies.
  • Fleet-wide governance with organization policy: Platform security leads can enforce compliance across their entire organization using custom organization policy constraints. You can use a constraint to reject any attempts to create a cluster that doesn't enable the Runtime Sensor add-on, which can prevent malicious actors from spinning up rogue infrastructure to evade runtime detection.
  • Kernel-level observability with minimal overhead: The Wiz Runtime Sensor continuously monitors system calls, running processes, network connections, and file access. It catches suspicious activity, including reverse shells, unauthorized privilege escalations, container escapes, and unsafe outbound connections while keeping CPU usage low even under heavy workload activity. 

    The sensor uses a fixed memory limit on each node to ensure consistent performance as workload density changes. This is especially valuable for AI workloads and web services where application activity might fluctuate quickly.
  • Independent auto-updates: Security threats and zero-day vulnerabilities don’t wait for scheduled infrastructure maintenance windows. The lifecycle of the Wiz sensor add-on for GKE is independent of your GKE cluster and node lifecycle. 

    The sensor periodically rolls out updates of new sensor versions published by Wiz, to help ensure that your clusters always have the latest detection rules without requiring GKE version bumps, node pool recreations, or workload disruption.

How it works: Deploying and enforcing the sensor

Enabling the Wiz sensor add-on follows the same process that platform administrators are already familiar with on GKE. Using standard gcloud commands, you can activate runtime protection during cluster creation, turn it on for existing clusters, and enforce it across your fleet while keeping credentials securely managed in Secret Manager.

Check the setup documentation for prerequisites, such as granting GKE access to Secret Manager.

Intelligent threat correlation for AI security

The true power of this integration emerges when the managed sensor connects to the broader Wiz AI Application Protection Platform (AI-APP). By feeding GKE runtime telemetry into the Wiz Security Graph, you unlock a security toolkit that goes beyond static alerting, with:

  • Real-time risk assessment and threat verification: By pairing background security scans with live activity monitoring, you get a clear view of real risks. The sensor checks whether vulnerable code is actually running in memory, so you can focus on active security threats and ignore inactive ones.
  • Real-time threat detection and response: Identify suspicious activity like malware, unauthorized access attempts, and software vulnerabilities in real time. Security teams can set rules to automatically block or stop threats before they can spread.
  • Network activity and detailed security insights: Track system activity, network connections, and data flows to uncover hidden risks and unauthorized software usage. If a threat is detected, the sensor automatically gathers diagnostic data to help teams quickly investigate what happened.

Together, these capabilities ensure that mission-critical applications and AI agents deployed on GKE are monitored for attacks and data exfiltration without compromising developer velocity.

Get started today

The Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for GKE delivers a standard for container security: deep, kernel-level eBPF protection without operational complexity or deployment friction.

By combining GKE's managed platform automation with Wiz's comprehensive security intelligence, platform and security teams can innovate at cloud speed while maintaining strong runtime defense. Check out the Wiz Sensor for GKE documentation to learn more.

entries.content:
Casey West

Developer Relations Lead, AI Infrastructure & Applied Engineering, Google Cloud

The real challenge of building an agentic system isn't the construction, it's the measurement.

Evaluation engineering is a critical foundation for building reliable AI systems. Setting up systematic, repeatable tests to measure your agent’s true behavior can be the difference between shipping a tool you can trust and one that silently breaks, fails to call APIs, or makes mistakes.

I’ve run evaluation engineering initiatives for years at Google and developing the newly released Google Cloud Developer plugin served as a live testbed to stress-test these key principles across real-world developer workflows.

Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds.

1. Grade the execution steps instead of the summary

When we first evaluated agents, we set up an LLM-as-judge to inspect the agent’s final text reply and scored it against a checklist. However, we quickly realized it’s fundamentally flawed because the grader only sees what the agent wrote, not what it actually did. When we ran our initial 11-prompt evaluation suite for the Google Cloud Developer plugin, the automated grader marked it as failing three prompts. But when we opened the raw tool-call logs and read the transcripts, the plugin had actually passed all three. On a Cloud Run cleanup prompt, for instance, our rubric required checking command syntax before running anything. The agent ran gcloud help run services list as its very first step. It did the work, but its final message was focused on warning the user about permanent data loss rather than reciting that it had checked the help docs.

The grader penalized the agent for doing the right thing simply because it didn’t brag about it in the summary. If your rubric line says "did it run X?", a LLM judge is guessing unless you evaluate the actual tool-call trajectory.

Takeaway: Don't grade an agent on its closing pitch. Score the raw execution trajectory to verify what commands were actually executed, validated, and scoped.

2. Design evals for asynchronous operations

When you start reading tool-call trajectories, how you extract that telemetry matters just as much as what you're reading. Extracting agent telemetry into a flattened, sequential list of events obscures concurrent tool dispatch, which is one of the critical causes of behavioral failure. Modern agent harnesses often batch multiple tool invocations into a single assistant turn using an array of calls.

In our evaluations, when an agent was asked to inspect an environment and look up documentation, the harness dispatched the skill-loading call and two documentation searches simultaneously within a single tool_calls payload. Because activating a skill is a multi-stage process, where the initial call returns a short launch stub and the subsequent turn injects the full instruction body, the instructions meant to govern the search arrived in the prompt context after the system had already executed the searches.

The system never gave the skill a dedicated turn to let its guidance influence the agent's actions. If telemetry pipelines strip out turn structures and merge calls into a flat timeline, engineers will waste days wondering why an agent disregarded unambiguous instructions that a developer embedded in a skill.

Takeaway: Preserve turn structure in telemetry extractors so you can identify when client-side parallel dispatch issues tool calls before injected guidance enters the context window.

3. Test live runs and "dry runs" side-by-side

You need to inspect real API calls to catch harness quirks, like parallel dispatch. But if you only test your agent in one environment condition, you're flying half-blind. From day one, you need to run two conditions side-by-side: a live run and a plan-only run. In the live condition, the agent has real, sandboxed credentials and actually executes commands. This is how you see if syntax works, parameters serialize cleanly, and the agent exercises restraint before doing something destructive.

Live runs frequently hit an unexpected permission error on step two and abort before you ever reach the behavior you’re trying to test. That's why you need the plan-only condition, where you strip credentials and tell the agent to explain what it would do without running anything. This strips out permission roadblocks and shows you the model’s pure reasoning and routing intent. Roughly half our most important findings came from the delta between the two.

For example, on one of our onboarding prompts, a live run was blocked immediately on a project list call. The plan-only run sailed right through and produced an 8,000-character plan that completely ignored organization policies, admin approvals, and governance. The live run masked a major cognitive flaw that the plan-only run exposed in seconds.

Takeaway: Run live and plan-only evaluations side by side. Live runs test actual execution and safety restraint; plan-only runs expose the model's raw reasoning and routing without getting tripped up by permission errors.

4. Use “golden sets” as durable baselines

Frontier model architectures change every few months, agent harnesses improve, and plugin manifest standards will inevitably evolve. When building the Google Cloud Developer plugin, we treated evaluations as continuous integration testing for these non-deterministic environments. That means we stress-tested the composite stack, including the harness, the live model, and the tools running together on realistic tasks.

Instead of guessing from the final text output, this approach captures the whole trajectory: what the agent thought, what commands it actually ran, and whether it solved the problem without breaking anything. Then you score that run against golden sets curated by real human experts who know what the ideal path looks like.

Takeaway: Build golden sets based on what the entire system should actually do in the wild, including your harness, model, and plugins. Models change, but those baseline runs are your safety net.

Reminder: Use evaluation suites over “one-shot” demos

A common mistake I see among engineers is what I like to call the one-shot demo. This is when someone feeds a prompt into a LLM, watches it build a complete 3D game or solves a Rubik’s cube in a single pass and calls it an eval. But in reality, this is just a vanity metric.

To do quality work with AI, I truly believe that you need evaluation suites. Without evaluations, teams are like literally running into a dark cave blind. Engineering an enterprise-grade agent means testing the system's ability to handle multi-step interactions, manage permissions, and avoid destructive outcomes like accidentally deleting a project because you asked it to "find opportunities to save costs."

Where to go from here

Building an agent plugin or MCP server is the beginning. Shipping something you can actually trust with real cloud infrastructure requires significantly more work in evaluations to ensure it’s doing what you expect it to do. At the end of the day, the only thing that outlasts model churn is a stress-tested eval suite. Check out the Google Cloud Developer plugin documentation or explore this codelab to get started with the plugin in Antigravity.
